title: Agreeing a price today
objectives: Draw the payoff of a forward contract at delivery.

screens.prose: A baker agrees today to buy one tonne of wheat from a miller in six months, at £200.00. No money changes hands today. Six months later, wheat trades at £230.00 a tonne.

params.xLabel: Wheat price at delivery (£ a tonne)

screens.question: What is the agreement worth to the baker on the delivery day?

widget.label: Value of the agreement on delivery day

hints.text: What could the baker do with the wheat the moment it arrives?
The baker pays £200.00 and receives wheat the market values at £230.00.
Sell it at once: $230 - 200 = 30$.

feedback.correct: The baker pays £200.00 for wheat worth £230.00: a gain of £30.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what the wheat is worth with what the baker pays for it.

byKey.whole: You counted the whole wheat price. The baker still pays £200.00, so only the difference is a gain.
byKey.paid: You subtracted the wrong way round. Paying £200.00 for wheat worth £230.00 is a gain.
byKey.none: You valued the deal by what changed hands today. By delivery day the fixed price has become a bargain.
byKey.price: That is what the baker pays, not what the deal is worth. Wheat worth £230.00 arrives for £200.00.

explain.text: The baker pays £200.00 for wheat worth £230.00, a gain of £30.00. The bold line shows that gain at every wheat price. At £230.00 it reads 30.

screens.prose: Slide the wheat price at delivery and watch the dot on the bold line. Its label shows what the agreement is worth to the baker. Take the price below £200.00.

params.xLabel: Wheat price at delivery (£ a tonne)

screens.question: What is the agreement worth to the baker when wheat ends at £170.00?

options.text: −£30.00: the baker must still pay £200.00 for wheat worth £170.00
£0.00: the baker walks away and buys at the market
options.why: You treated the agreement as an option. The baker signed a promise to buy, so the loss below £200.00 is real.
You took the size of the move and dropped its sign. Paying £200.00 for £170.00 of wheat loses money.

feedback.correct: Below £200.00 the baker overpays, so the payoff is negative.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide the price to £170.00 and read the label on the dot.

explain.text: At £170.00 the baker pays £200.00 for wheat worth £170.00, a loss of £30.00. The line keeps falling below £200.00: it has no floor. Each £1.00 on the wheat price moves the payoff by £1.00.

screens.prose: This agreement is a **forward contract**. The fixed price is the **forward price** $F$, paid on the **delivery date** $T$. The baker, who will buy, is **long** the forward. The miller, who will sell, is **short**. Here is the miller's side.

params.xLabel: Wheat price at delivery (£ a tonne)

screens.question: What is the miller's payoff when wheat ends at £230.00?

widget.placeholder: a number of pounds; negative for a loss
widget.label: Miller's payoff at delivery

hints.text: Could the miller have sold the wheat for more elsewhere?
The miller hands over wheat worth £230.00 and receives £200.00.

feedback.correct: The miller sells £230.00 of wheat for £200.00: $F - S_T = -30$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what the miller receives with what the wheat is worth.

byKey.copied: You gave the miller the baker's payoff. The miller sells £230.00 of wheat for £200.00, which loses £30.00.
byKey.zero: You assumed the seller just collects the fixed price, so nothing is lost. The miller could have sold at £230.00 instead.
byKey.price: That is the cash the miller receives. The payoff compares it with the £230.00 the wheat is worth.

explain.text: The miller hands over wheat worth £230.00 for £200.00, so the payoff is $F - S_T = 200 - 230 = -30$. The miller's line is the baker's line flipped. One side's gain is the other side's loss.

screens.prose: The forward price is $F = \text{£}200.00$. Fill in both sides' payoffs at delivery for four wheat prices. Use negative numbers for losses.

params.xLabel: Wheat price at delivery (£ a tonne)

screens.question: Fill in the long and the short payoff at each price.

hints.text: For each price, ask who would rather have traded at the market.
At £200.00 the wheat is worth exactly what is paid for it.
Long: $-30, 0, 15, 40$. Short: the same numbers with the sign flipped.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The long gets $S_T - 200$, the short $200 - S_T$, losses negative.

byKey.r0c1: At £170.00 the long pays £200.00 for wheat worth £170.00. That is a loss, so the entry is negative.
byKey.r1c1: At $S_T = F$ the long pays exactly what the wheat is worth. Neither side gains.
byKey.r2c1: At £215.00 the long buys for £200.00 wheat worth £215.00.
byKey.r3c1: At £240.00 the long buys for £200.00 wheat worth £240.00.
byKey.r0c2: At £170.00 the short sells for £200.00 wheat worth only £170.00: a gain.
byKey.r1c2: At $S_T = F$ the short receives exactly what the wheat is worth. Neither side gains.
byKey.r2c2: At £215.00 the short gives up wheat worth £215.00 for £200.00.
byKey.r3c2: At £240.00 the short gives up wheat worth £240.00 for £200.00.

explain.text: Each row adds to zero: what the long gains, the short loses. At £200.00 both payoffs are 0, the edge where the deal is exactly fair. A forward moves money between the two sides and creates none.

screens.prose: Back to signing day. The baker and the miller agree $F = \text{£}200.00$ for delivery in six months. Wheat trades at £195.00 today.

params.xLabel: Wheat price at delivery (£ a tonne)

screens.question: How much does the baker pay the miller when they sign?

options.why: You paid the forward price today. $F$ is paid on the delivery date, when the wheat arrives.
You bought the wheat at today's price. Nobody buys wheat today; they fix the price of a later sale.

options.text: A small fee, like an option premium
options.why: You treated the forward as an option. Both sides are bound, so neither buys a right and neither pays for one.

hints.text: When does the wheat change hands?
The £200.00 is paid in exchange for the wheat.
Signing creates two promises and moves no cash. Everything happens on the delivery date.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what is exchanged on signing day, and what on delivery day.

byKey.pays-f: You paid the forward price today. $F$ is paid on the delivery date, in exchange for the wheat.
byKey.premium: You treated the forward as an option. A forward gives no choice, so there is nothing to pay for.

explain.text: A forward costs nothing to enter: each side takes on an obligation, and neither pays the other. The £200.00 moves on the delivery date, with the wheat. Lesson 10 shows how $F$ is set so that zero is the fair price to enter.

screens.prose: Now draw the baker's payoff yourself. The forward price is £200.00. Drag each blue point up or down to the payoff at that wheat price.
screens.question: Draw the baker's payoff at delivery from £160.00 to £240.00.

hints.text: What is the payoff at £160.00? Below the forward price, the baker still has to buy.
At £200.00 the payoff is 0, and it changes by £1.00 for each £1.00 of wheat price.
The points sit at −40, −20, 0, 20 and 40: one straight line through £200.00.

feedback.correct: A straight line through £200.00, falling below zero on the left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. At each point, work out $S_T - 200$, including below £200.00.

byKey.floor: You drew a floor at zero, as for a call. The baker must buy at £200.00 even when wheat is cheaper, so the line keeps falling.
byKey.short: You drew the miller's side. The baker gains when wheat rises.

explain.text: The forward payoff is the straight line $S_T - 200$, negative below £200.00. A floor at zero would need a right to walk away. That right is an option, and it costs a premium.

screens.prose: You found the payoffs price by price. For a forward with price $F$, at delivery: $$\text{long: } S_T - F, \qquad \text{short: } F - S_T.$$ Both are straight lines through $F$, with slopes 1 and −1 and no floor. They always add to zero.
screens.question: A long forward has $F = \text{£}50.00$. At what price at delivery does it pay $-\text{£}10.00$?

options.why: You solved $F - S_T = -10$, the short's payoff. For the long, $S_T - 50 = -10$.

options.text: Never: it cannot pay less than £0.00
options.why: You gave the forward a floor. Only an option has one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the long's payoff $S_T - 50$ equal to $-10$.

explain.text: The long pays $S_T - 50$, which equals $-10$ when $S_T = 40$. Below the forward price the long loses one for one. The loss stops only at $S_T = 0$, where it is $-F$.

screens.prose: A farmer will harvest one tonne of wheat in six months. To fix her selling price she goes short a forward at £200.00. At delivery she holds the crop, worth $S_T$, and the short forward.

params.xLabel: Wheat price at delivery (£ a tonne)
params.label: crop + forward

screens.question: What does the farmer hold in total at delivery, whatever the wheat price?

hints.text: Add the two pieces at one price, say £175.00.
At £175.00 the crop is worth £175.00 and the short forward pays $200 - 175 = 25$.
$S_T + (200 - S_T) = 200$ at every price.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the crop's value and the short forward's payoff.

byKey.spot: That is the crop alone at £175.00. Add the short forward, which pays $200 - 175 = 25$.
byKey.fwd: That is the forward alone. She also holds the crop, worth £175.00.
byKey.zero: The forward cancels the risk, not the value. She still sells a tonne of wheat.

explain.text: The crop is worth $S_T$ and the short forward pays $200 - S_T$, so together they are worth £200.00. The bold line is flat: the wheat price no longer matters to her. A forward on something you already hold cancels your exposure to its price.

screens.prose: A UK importer must pay a US supplier 1,000,000 US dollars in three months. A bank offers a three-month forward at £0.7900 per dollar, and the importer goes long. In three months a dollar costs £0.8200 at the market.

params.xLabel: Pounds per US dollar in three months

screens.question: What does the invoice cost the importer in pounds, counting the forward's payoff?

widget.label: Net cost of the invoice
widget.accept: £790,000.00, the forward rate times the amount

hints.text: Price the dollars at the market first, then add what the forward pays.
The forward pays $(0.82 - 0.79) \times 1{,}000{,}000$ pounds.
Dollars cost £820,000.00; the forward pays £30,000.00; the net is £790,000.00.

feedback.correct: £820,000.00 at the market, less the forward's £30,000.00: £790,000.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Buy the dollars at £0.8200, then subtract the forward's payoff.

byKey.spot: That is the cost without the forward. The forward pays £30,000.00, which brings the cost down.
byKey.payoff: That is the forward's payoff alone. The importer still has to buy 1,000,000 dollars.
byKey.added: You added the payoff as a cost. The forward pays the importer when the dollar rises.

explain.text: At the market the dollars cost £820,000.00, and the forward pays $(0.82 - 0.79) \times 1{,}000{,}000 = \text{£}30{,}000.00$. Net, the invoice costs £790,000.00, fixed on the day of the deal. Had the dollar fallen, the forward would lose exactly what the cheaper dollars saved.

screens.prose: A trader is long a forward on a share at $F = \text{£}100.00$. She also buys a put struck at £100.00, expiring on the delivery date. Ignore what the put cost. The bold line is the two together.
screens.question: Which single contract has the same payoff as the two together?

options.why: You kept the forward's slope everywhere. Below £100.00 the put's gain cancels the forward's loss, so the line goes flat.
A short put loses below the strike and is flat above it. This pair is flat below and rises above.
Moving the forward price keeps a straight line. This pair has a kink at £100.00.

hints.text: Read the bold line below £100.00 and above it.
Below £100.00 the put pays $100 - S_T$ and the forward pays $S_T - 100$.
Below £100.00 the two cancel to 0. Above, only the forward pays: $S_T - 100$. Which contract pays $\max(S_T - 100, 0)$?

feedback.correct: Flat at 0 below £100.00 and $S_T - 100$ above: a call.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the total payoff at £90.00 and at £110.00.

byKey.share: You kept the forward's slope everywhere. Below £100.00 the put's gain cancels the forward's loss.

explain.text: Below £100.00 the put pays $100 - S_T$ and the forward $S_T - 100$: together 0. Above, only the forward pays, so the total is $\max(S_T - 100, 0)$, a call. This link between forwards, puts and calls is put-call parity, in level 3 of the options course.

ideas: A forward fixes today the price $F$ of a trade on a later date. No money changes hands until then.
At delivery the long gets $S_T - F$ and the short $F - S_T$: straight lines through $F$, with no floor.
A forward on something you already hold, or must buy, fixes its price and cancels your exposure.

formula.name: Forward payoff at delivery
formula.note: Both sides are bound. The two payoffs add to zero.

summary.trap: A forward is not an option. Its payoff keeps falling below $F$; a floor at zero would need a right to walk away.

quiz.prose: You are long a forward on a share at $F = \text{£}80.00$. On the delivery date the share trades at £72.50.
quiz.question: What is your payoff?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The long's payoff is $S_T - F$.

byKey.sign: You took $F - S_T$, the short's payoff. You must buy at £80.00 a share worth £72.50.
byKey.floor: You gave the forward a floor. You are bound to buy, so the loss stands.
byKey.price: You counted the whole forward price as lost. You also receive the share, worth £72.50.

explain.text: You pay £80.00 for a share worth £72.50, so the payoff is $S_T - F = -7.50$. There is no option to walk away.

quiz.prose: A fund is short a forward on 500 shares at £40.00 a share. On the delivery date the share trades at £46.00.
quiz.question: What is the fund's total payoff?

widget.label: Total payoff of the short forward

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the short's payoff per share, $F - S_T$, then multiply by 500.

byKey.sign: You used the long's payoff. The fund sells at £40.00 shares worth £46.00, which loses.
byKey.per: That is the payoff per share. The forward covers 500 shares.

explain.text: Per share the short gets $F - S_T = 40 - 46 = -6$. On 500 shares that is −£3,000.00.

quiz.prose: An airline goes long a forward on 1,000 tonnes of jet fuel at £600.00 a tonne. At delivery fuel trades at £540.00 a tonne. The airline buys its fuel at the market and settles the forward.
quiz.question: What does the fuel cost the airline in total, counting the forward?

feedback.correct: £540,000.00 at the market plus the forward's £60,000.00 loss: £600,000.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the market cost and the forward's loss.

byKey.spot: That ignores the forward. It loses $1{,}000 \times (540 - 600) = -60{,}000$, which the airline pays.
byKey.payoff: That is the forward's payoff alone. The airline still buys 1,000 tonnes of fuel.
byKey.sign: You subtracted the forward's loss. A loss adds to what the airline pays.

explain.text: The fuel costs £540,000.00 at the market, and the forward loses £60,000.00. In total the airline pays £600,000.00, the price it locked in. It gave up the saving from cheaper fuel in exchange for certainty.

quiz.prose: Two firms sign a one-year forward on a share at $F = \text{£}25.00$.
quiz.question: Which statement is true on the day they sign?

options.text: No money changes hands, and both firms are bound to trade in a year
The buyer pays £25.00 now and receives the share in a year
options.why: You paid the forward price at signing. It is paid on the delivery date.

options.text: The buyer may walk away in a year if the share is below £25.00
options.why: You gave the buyer a choice. That is a call option; a forward binds both sides.

options.text: The seller pays the buyer a fee for the obligation
options.why: You priced the promise as if one side were doing the other a favour. Entering a forward costs neither side anything.

feedback.correct: A forward is two promises and no cash today.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what a forward obliges each side to do, and when.

explain.text: Signing a forward creates an obligation on both sides and moves no money. In a year the buyer pays £25.00 and the seller delivers the share, whatever its price.
